messages.subject: Question about plyr and ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hello, everyone.

I am looking at the posterior mean as a function of the sample mean
(xbar) from an IID normal distribution with mean theta and variance
1.  This is a Bayesian problem, so I have a proper Uniform(a,b) prior
on theta. Also, I'm denoting the sample size as n.

Explicitly, the posterior mean for a given (xbar, n, a, b)-tuple is

posterior.mean <- function(xbar, n, a, b) {
	post.mean <- xbar + (1 / n) * ((dnorm(xbar - b) - dnorm(xbar - a)) /
(pnorm(b - xbar) - pnorm(a - xbar)))
	return(post.mean)
}

I am using adply to look at the posterior mean as a function of xbar
for a few sample sizes.  Note that I am using a = 10 and b = 20.  My
code for this is given here.

a <- 10
b <- 20

sample.sizes <- c(5, 10, 20, 50)
xbar <- seq(10, 20, by = 0.1)

post.mean.df <- adply(sample.sizes, 1, function(n) {
	data.frame(n = n, xbar = xbar, post.mean = posterior.mean(xbar, n, a,
b))
})

My issue is that I am not getting what I expect when I plot the
resulting data frame using ggplot2.

p <- ggplot(post.mean.df, aes(x = xbar, y = post.mean, group = n))
p <- p + geom_line(aes(color = n))
p <- p + labs(x = expression(bar(X)), y = "Posterior Mean")
p

I expect to see 4 plots, one for each sample size, labeled as 5, 10,
20, and 50. Instead, I am seeing 5 plots with labels 10, 20, 30, 40,
50.

I suspect that my problem is in my ggplot2 code because the data frame
appears to be okay.  However, I gave all of the code in case anyone
can identify my problem.  Any thoughts?

Thank you in advance.

John Ramey

messages.subject: MC slower than one core?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm a new plyr fan, after it was shown to me that it is much faster
than other functions I can write myself.

I'm writing to ask about the comment in the plyr announcement about
parallel (pasted below).  Is it a mirage?  The parallel version
multicore actually takes 3 times longer.

If there were some calculations going on in this example, I would
suspect competition over cores between R multicore and an external
linear algebra package.  I've seen bad R multicore performance when an
external BLAS (like GotoBLAS2) is in use and there is no restriction
on the number of threads in use.  The BLAS uses threads, and it gets
into a fight with multicore for control.  I imagine like a "stampede"
at the door of a burning building. One person, OK. Two people, OK. 30
people?  Logjam with 3 people wedged in the opening.

But in this case, well, I have no explanation.

>From Plyr announcement:

NEW FEATURES

* l*ply, d*ply, a*ply and m*ply all gain a .parallel argument that
when TRUE,
 applies functions in parallel using a parallel backend registered
with the
 foreach package:

 x <- seq_len(20)
 wait <- function(i) Sys.sleep(0.1)
 system.time(llply(x, wait))
 #  user  system elapsed
 # 0.007   0.005   2.005

 library(doMC)
 registerDoMC(2)
 system.time(llply(x, wait, .parallel = TRUE))
 #  user  system elapsed
 # 0.020   0.011   1.038

Paul E. Johnson
Professor, Political Science
University of Kansas

messages.subject_clean: Data type treating column and row ID variables symmetrically?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone!

Does anybody knows of an data type and manipulation facilities for data tables
with multiple column variables as in the following example:

|     |     | a | a | a | b | b |  <- cv1
|     |     | c | c | d | d | e |  <- cv2
|-----+-----+---+---+---+---+---|
| x   | v   | 5 | 5 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| x   | W   | 8 | 5 | 0 | 1 | 7 |
| y   | v   | 5 | 2 | 6 | 1 | 2 |
| z   | v   | 6 | 9 | 1 | 9 | 7 |
| z   | W   | 0 | 0 | 7 | 6 | 6 |
  ^     ^
 rv1   rv3

Here cv1 and cv2 are column ID variables (vary by column).

Row ID variables are rv1 and rv2 (vary by rows).

Data.frame is limited in this respect,  it does not distinguish between
row/column ID variables' names and  allow only for one column variable.

Reshape package overcomes partially this problem by pasting the column variables
(cv1, cv2) into one with "_" separator.

So to be more precise, what would be the easiest strategy to
(1) import such data, and
(2) reshape it into the long form?

Preferably an automated tool designed specifically to this type of problems. Does
exist any? Reshape comes close but still requires quite some computation.

(3) Also an export tool to the rectangular format as above? It's many times useful
to present your data in a user-friendly way.

Many thanks for any suggestions,
Vitally.

After a little trial and error, I came up with this:

# Attempt to use read.ftable():

# File prep:
Input file (pipes stripped, column labels quoted, some other stuff, per example(read.ftable):
[tedious!]

"           \'a\'  \'a\'  \'a\'  \'b\'  \'b\' \n",
"           \'c\'  \'c\'  \'d\'  \'d\'  \'e\' \n",
" x    v    5  5  1  1  2 \n",
" x    W    8  5  0  1  7 \n",
" y    v    5  2  6  1  2 \n",
" z    v    6  9  1  9  7 \n",
" z    W    0  0  7  6  6 \n",

(By the way, why do you have two columns labeled 'a c'?
Shouldn't they be merged, or is the second meant to be 'b c' ?)

# R code:

temp <- tempfile()
cat("           \'a\'  \'a\'  \'a\'  \'b\'  \'b\' \n",
"           \'c\'  \'c\'  \'d\'  \'d\'  \'e\' \n",
" x    v    5  5  1  1  2 \n",
" x    W    8  5  0  1  7 \n",
" y    v    5  2  6  1  2 \n",
" z    v    6  9  1  9  7 \n",
" z    W    0  0  7  6  6 \n", file = temp)
file.show(temp)
ft <- read.ftable(temp, skip = 2, row.var.names = list(c('F1', 'F2')),
            col.vars = list('F3' = c('a', 'b'),
                            'F4' = c('c', 'd', 'e')))
Warning message:
In read.ftable(temp, skip = 2, row.var.names = list(c("F1", "F2")),  :
  NAs introduced by coercion
> ft
              F3  a        b
              F4  c  d  e  c  d  e
c("F1", "F2")
'x'              NA  5  5  1  1  2
'y'              NA  8  5  0  1  7
'z'              NA  5  2  6  1  2

Not quite - it seems that three variables is the limit for read.ftable(). (Things weren't any different when I used
row.var.names = c('F1', 'F2') other than a second column of c('x', 'x', 'x').)

Back to the drawing board - this time we create a data frame and build an ftable from that.

# Plan B:
# Make vectors of the factor levels
> f1 <- c('x', 'y', 'z')
> f2 <- c('v', 'W')
> f3 <- c('a', 'b')
> f4 <- c('c', 'd', 'e')
# Use expand.grid() to get their combinations

# I had my reasons for doing this at the time, but...
df <- expand.grid(f3 = f3, f4 = f4, f1 = f1, f2 = f2)

# Now create the vector of frequencies that correspond to these particular combinations:

It has to do with reshape more than with anything else in this world.

Here is the example taken from reshape2 for "dcast":

names(ChickWeight) <- tolower(names(ChickWeight))
chick_m <- melt(ChickWeight, id=2:4, na.rm=TRUE)
dcast(chick_m, time ~ variable + diet, mean) # average effect of time

Here is the casted data:

   time  weight_1 weight_2 weight_3 weight_4
1     0  41.40000     40.7     40.8  41.0000
2     2  47.25000     49.4     50.4  51.8000
3     4  56.47368     59.8     62.2  64.5000
4     6  66.78947     75.4     77.9  83.9000

As you can see two ID variables ("variable" and "diet") are now column.variables,
but they are pasted together with "_" separator and mixed with the label
"time". "time" is an ID row.variable here.
This limitation of data.frame format is the source of all the confusion and the
reason reshape package does not have an intuitive appeal for many people.

Equivalently the data could be displayed with variables "variable" and "diet" on
separate rows:

         variable    weight   weight   weight   weight
             diet         1        2        3        4
   time
1     0            41.40000     40.7     40.8  41.0000
2     2            47.25000     49.4     50.4  51.8000
3     4            56.47368     59.8     62.2  64.5000
4     6            66.78947     75.4     77.9  83.9000

This is strikingly similar to the format of "ftable" but it is not; ftable is
always balanced. In the rectangular representation above some levels of ID
variables could be missing.

This is the format people in the social sciences organize the experimental
data. Often the data is collected by hand, and it is easier to organize it in this
way.

So as you can see,  everything is entirely in the framework of "reshape" package.

This is common requirement for me to write my own import and export functions. I
will attend to it in the near feature.

I am curious what Hadley would say about adding two attributes to casted
data.frames similar to  "ftable" class:

 - attr(*, "row.vars")=List of 3
 - attr(*, "col.vars")=List of 1

given this information the print method could be developed for nice display of
casted data and import/export functionality easily added. Internally though it
will still be a data.frame:).

messages.subject: Re: Error in ddply
messages.body_plain:
I started getting the same error when I upgraded.

In my case, I appear to be causing the problem by passing something
like NewVariable='Value' among other things to a ddply function. This
sounds obscure, but here's an example.

I use ddply and cast functions to calculate the percent of total at
successive levels of aggregation and stick them together with cbind
and rbind:

bball <- subset(baseball, year > 1900 & lg %in% c('AL','NL'))
# randomly assign a fake handedness variable
bball$hand <- cut(runif(nrow(bball), min=0, max=1), c(0, .65, 0.9,
1.0), c("R","L","B"))

rbind(
	cast(ddply(bball, .(lg, year), summarise, hand = hand, pct = hr /
sum(hr)), lg+year~hand, sum)
	,
		cast(ddply(bball, .(year), summarise, lg = 'Both Leagues', hand =
hand, pct = hr / sum(hr)), year~hand, sum)
	)

In the example above, I am calculating the share of home runs by
handedness within each league, then stacking the results onto a
similar table that calculates the share for both leagues. To make the
rbind() work properly, I assigned  lg = 'Both Leagues' inside the
ddply statement. That appears to break now with the error message
cited above.

I can get the results I need by running the following:

rbind(
	cast(ddply(bball, .(lg, year), summarise, hand = hand, pct = hr /
sum(hr)), lg+year~hand, sum)
	,
	cbind(
		lg='Both Leagues',
		cast(ddply(bball, .(year), summarise, hand = hand, pct = hr /
sum(hr)), year~hand, sum)
	 )
	)

With such an easy workaround, this isn't a critical issue for me, but
I thought this might help others troubleshoot.

I am trying to update the graphics in my class notes with ggplot2.

they have equal length and width. The two distributions are
Uniform(0,2) and Uniform(3,5).

The plots look good, but I do not know how to change the fill colors.
I have been unsuccessful with a number of scale_fill_* variants. Any
thoughts?

a1 <- 0
b1 <- 2
a2 <- 3
b2 <- 5

x1 <- seq(a1, b1, by = 0.01)
x2 <- seq(a2, b2, by = 0.01)

y1 <- dunif(x1, a1, b1)
y2 <- dunif(x2, a2, b2)

df1 <- cbind.data.frame(x = x1, y = y1, Distribution = "Uniform(0,2)")
df2 <- cbind.data.frame(x = x2, y = y2, Distribution = "Uniform(3,5)")

df <- rbind(df1, df2)
df$Distribution <- factor(df$Distribution)

unif.loc.ggplot <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y, group = Distribution))
unif.loc.ggplot <- unif.loc.ggplot + geom_area(aes(fill =
Distribution))
unif.loc.ggplot <- unif.loc.ggplot + ylim(0.0, 1.0)
unif.loc.ggplot

Thanks in advance for any advice you can give.

Well, as usual Dennis, you have helped me reconceptualize the problem entirely!

Your example function (boot0) was very different than any way I was thinking about solving the problem.   I played with it for a while, and looked at your histogram plot and asked myself what did I really want out of my analysis?  I was really after the bootstrap median and ci’s.  At some point, I remembered that ggplot2 had some boot strapping built in to stat_summary.  I studied that, wrote something overly complicated using the functions from Hmisc, then boiled it down to this very lean code with the ggplot2 built-ins:

df <- data.frame(res = rnorm(30),
    gen = sample(c("A", "B"), 30, replace = T),
    trt = sample(c("H", "L"), 30, replace = T))

#### Really clean code, includes original data points as “freckles”

jit <- position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0.0)
p <- ggplot(data = df, aes(y = res, x = gen, color = gen))
p <- p + layer(geom = "jitter", position = jit, color = "black", size = 1)
p <- p + facet_grid(.~trt) + ylab("Bootstrap Mean +/- CI") + xlab("")
p <- p + stat_summary(fun.data = "median_hilow")
print(p)

The final answer is so compact and of course it shows how Hadley anticipated guys like me.  I’m a little embarassed – I didn’t mean to illustrate to the whole group the random-walk of my critical thinking skills!  When I see this evolution of thought-process in my students and the light “goes on”, I’m always pleased when they “get it”, but in myself...

A big thanks to Dennis, and a nod to the prescient Hadley!

Bryan

messages.subject: Having *ply functions "gracefully" handle errors?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Would it make sense to add something like an ".onerror=..." parameter
to the *ply functions so the user can "gracefully" recover from an
error thrown from one of the iterations in the *ply function w/o
hosing the entire computation?

For instance, say I have some long/complex code embedded in an ldply loop:

gene.stats <- ldply(genes, function(gene) {
  ## lots
  ## of
  ## computation
  ## here
  data.frame(gene=name(gene), something.x=some.calc.x,
something.y=some.calc.y, ...)
})

and for some reason (poor annotation on my part, some out of bounds
thing, etc.), the computation throws an error when doing its thing on
one (or a few) genes in my gene list, then my whole computation will
get hosed  due to small small edge case I didn't foresee.

Now imagine that the `.onerror` parameter took a function that was run
when some error happens in the *ply .fun parameter, like so:

gene.stats <- ldply(gene, function(gene) {
   ##
}, .onerror=function(e) data.frame(gene=name(gene), something.x=-1,
something.y=-1))

Now I can do my long computation, let it finish, and hunt for errors
by looking for `gene.stats$something.x==-1` to see what's causing me
grief later.

... after writing this message, I see that `.inform` kind of does this
by showing me what error is happening, but I'd like to just hop over
the error (especially on long-running *ply calls).

Maybe, conditionally wrapping line 71:
http://github.com/hadley/plyr/blob/master/R/ply-list.r#L71

with something like:

res <- tryCatch(.fun(piece, ...), error=.onerror)

would do the trick. And by "conditionally" I mean maybe you only run
the tryCatch code if !is.null(.onerror), or something so that we don't
incur the overhead of tryCatch if'n you don't set .onerror ...

Just a thought,
-steve

--

>>> On Monday, September 27, 2010, Steve Lianoglou
>>> <mailinglis...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>> Hi,
>>>>
>>>> Would it make sense to add something like an ".onerror=..." parameter
>>>> to the *ply functions so the user can "gracefully" recover from an
>>>> error thrown from one of the iterations in the *ply function w/o
>>>> hosing the entire computation?
>>>>
>>>> For instance, say I have some long/complex code embedded in an ldply loop:
>>>>
>>>> gene.stats <- ldply(genes, function(gene) {
>>>>   ## lots
>>>>   ## of
>>>>   ## computation
>>>>   ## here
>>>>   data.frame(gene=name(gene), something.x=some.calc.x,
>>>> something.y=some.calc.y, ...)
>>>> })
>>>>
>>>> and for some reason (poor annotation on my part, some out of bounds
>>>> thing, etc.), the computation throws an error when doing its thing on
>>>> one (or a few) genes in my gene list, then my whole computation will
>>>> get hosed  due to small small edge case I didn't foresee.
>>>>
>>>> Now imagine that the `.onerror` parameter took a function that was run
>>>> when some error happens in the *ply .fun parameter, like so:
>>>>
>>>> gene.stats <- ldply(gene, function(gene) {
>>>>    ##
>>>> }, .onerror=function(e) data.frame(gene=name(gene), something.x=-1,
>>>> something.y=-1))
>>>>
>>>> Now I can do my long computation, let it finish, and hunt for errors
>>>> by looking for `gene.stats$something.x==-1` to see what's causing me
>>>> grief later.
>>>>
>>>> ... after writing this message, I see that `.inform` kind of does this
>>>> by showing me what error is happening, but I'd like to just hop over
>>>> the error (especially on long-running *ply calls).
>>>>
>>>> Maybe, conditionally wrapping line 71:
>>>> http://github.com/hadley/plyr/blob/master/R/ply-list.r#L71
>>>>
>>>> with something like:
>>>>
>>>> res <- tryCatch(.fun(piece, ...), error=.onerror)
>>>>
>>>> would do the trick. And by "conditionally" I mean maybe you only run
>>>> the tryCatch code if !is.null(.onerror), or something so that we don't
>>>> incur the overhead of tryCatch if'n you don't set .onerror ...
>>>>
>>>> Just a thought,
